explanation: The colon explains the process: a technician tests parts one by one until the faulty one is identified. That means singling out, or isolating, the source of the problem. "Adapting" or "incorporating" a malfunction's source makes no sense, and "fabricating" would mean inventing it.

fix.passage: ______ the source of a malfunction in a complex electrical system can be a painstaking, time-consuming process: a repair technician may need to test each individual component one by one until the specific part causing the problematic behavior is identified.

explanation: The text goes on to describe organisms that adjust their internal electrolyte concentrations in response to outside changes, which is what it means to regulate internal salt levels. "Tolerate" is tempting, but the example is about actively controlling salt, not just enduring it; "counteract" and "elude" don't fit an object like "internal salt levels."

Most studies focus on people living above sea level, but these researchers "instead" studied people living below sea level. Taking a new, unusual direction is an innovative path. "Predictable" and "timeworn" suggest the opposite, and nothing in the text suggests the choice was "idealistic."

"While once" sets up a contrast with the claim that basic training "cannot provide enough protection" today. So the training used to be adequate, or sufficient. "Superficial" doesn't create a contrast, and "uncommon" and "affordable" have nothing to do with how much protection the training gave.

The semicolon is followed by an explanation: the design rejected ornate decoration in favor of clean lines and simplicity. A plain, unadorned style is austere. "Ostentatious" means showy, the opposite, while "capricious" (unpredictable) and "convoluted" (overly complicated) don't match "simplicity."

The passage focuses on the man's body and behavior as he nears the meeting: he breathes hard though he hasn't been galloping, rides slower and slower, sweats, and looks at the cabin as if approaching an unexploded shell. All of these details show his nervousness. The howitzer image is a comparison describing his expression, not a real earlier experience, so B is wrong.

fix.passage:
The following text is adapted from the 1940 novel The Hamlet by William Faulkner. In Mississippi, a man is riding a horse toward the residence of someone he intends to meet with about a business matter.

He was breathing hard but not because he had been galloping. On the contrary, since he had approached near enough to his destination to believe he could have seen smoke if there had been smoke, he had ridden slower and slower. Nevertheless he now sat the horse before the gap in the fence, breathing hard enough through his nose and even sweating a little, looking at the sagging broken-backed cabin set in its inevitable treeless and grassless plot and weathered to the color of an old bee-hive, with that expression of tense and rapid speculation of a man approaching a dud howitzer [artillery] shell.

explanation: The text names several forestry careers (arborists, researchers, ecologists) and stresses that each combines science with practical work. That matches D. The text never discusses technological advances (A) or job security (C), and it doesn't analyze specific environmental challenges in detail (B).

The first sentence praises wetlands for filtering pollutants as well as treatment plants. The underlined sentence begins with "However" and explains that overloading wetlands with industrial runoff can weaken that filtering, so it limits the earlier praise. It doesn't describe a measurement method, criticize treatment plants, or refute a hypothesis.

In the graph, Ethiopia has 5 volcanoes active since 1960 while Tanzania has only 1, so Ethiopia has more. Ethiopia has 10 volcanoes active since 1800 versus Tanzania's 3, so A and B are wrong, and D reverses the 1960 comparison.

The underlined claim is that cyberpunk is largely about style (aesthetic) rather than ideas. A critic saying that cyberpunk's defining feature is a fondness for 1980s pop-culture objects like mirrored sunglasses directly supports that, since it defines the genre by look and style. Choice C criticizes Shurin's definition as too broad, but it says nothing about cyberpunk being aesthetic, and B actually stresses ideas and themes.

fix.passage: Editor Jared Shurin’s enormous 2023 anthology The Big Book of Cyberpunk comprises 108 stories. Shurin’s volume is chronologically expansive, featuring such stories as James Tiptree Jr.’s “The Girl Who Was Plugged In” (1973) and Erica Satifka’s “Act of Providence” (2021). In his introduction, Shurin defines cyberpunk as a subgenre of speculative fiction concerning “the influence of technology on the scale, the pace, or the pattern of human affairs”; however, some critics assert that <u>cyberpunk is a literary movement that is in large part aesthetic rather than idea driven.</u>

choices.A: “Not all the stories anthologized in The Big Book of Cyberpunk were first published as stand-alone short stories in magazines or journals: for example, qntm’s 2021 story ‘Lena’ was originally self-published on the author’s site qntm.org.”

note: Solver answer was C; C criticizes the breadth of Shurin's definition but doesn't support the 'aesthetic rather than idea driven' claim. D does.

The claim is that the plan depends on Neoptolemus not having been among those who abandoned Philoctetes. In C, Odysseus explains why Neoptolemus can approach Philoctetes safely when he himself cannot: Neoptolemus did not sail "with the foremost band." The other quotations are about deceit, scouting, or staying hidden, not about Neoptolemus's absence from the earlier abandonment.

The text stresses that much of the novel is "pure invention." Readers who focus only on links to Céline's real life would therefore overlook how much he made up, which means missing his creativity. C is the reverse of the problem described, and the text never discusses earlier writers (B) or readership (D).

Consumer expectations keep rising, and even a promising solution like self-service lockers creates new problems. It follows that companies will need to keep trying new approaches to keep up. D goes too far by predicting that locker innovation will stall, and C contradicts the text's point that companies are actively looking for advances.

"That many travelers recommend" is a restrictive clause identifying which kind of city Nicosia is, so it takes "that" with no comma. D wrongly puts a comma before "that," A uses a nonrestrictive "which" clause that doesn't fit "one European city," and B ("in which") creates an ungrammatical clause.

The first part of the sentence, "As nanotechnology evolves," is in the present tense and describes an ongoing process, so the result should be in the future: medical technology "will likely continue" to evolve. The past perfect and conditional forms in A, B, and C don't match the present-tense context.

The phrase "adding a stiffened leather sole and hardened toe box" is an interruption that opens with a dash after "made," so it must close with a matching dash. Then the main verb "began" follows. A comma, a colon, or no punctuation would not properly close the dash-set phrase.

The text after the blank is a list explaining what "threefold" means, so a colon is right: "threefold: to provide..., to reflect..., and to develop...." A and C would leave the list as a fragment standing on its own, and D runs the list into the main clause without any punctuation.

"Extensive radiocarbon dating... confirmed... the Peruvian site's age" is a complete sentence, and the next part explains what that age was, which is a good job for a colon. A creates a comma splice between two independent clauses, and C and D join them without proper punctuation.

The subject is the plural "applications" ("Commercial applications of this new synthetic dye technology"), so the verb must be plural: "were." The interrupting phrase about mauve doesn't change the subject. "Was," "is," and "has been" are singular and agree with "technology" or "mauve" by mistake.

The text describes a sequence of steps ("First," then cooling, then droplets, then "Finally"). The droplet stage comes between the cooling and the final step, so "Next" fits. "Lastly" can't be used before "Finally," and "Similarly" and "Instead" don't show a sequence.

The previous sentence says the fungi "serve as a defense mechanism," and this sentence explains exactly how: by fighting diseases and boosting the tree's immune system. A more detailed explanation is introduced by "Specifically." "Nevertheless" signals contrast and "In conclusion" signals a summary, neither of which fits.

The first sentence gives the long-held hypothesis of a steppe origin; the second presents new evidence for a different origin. That contrast calls for "However." "Consequently" would wrongly suggest the new evidence resulted from the old hypothesis.

explanation: Farmers must consider each factor both on its own and in terms of how the factors "affect each other." That mutual influence is an interplay. "Neglect," "misinterpretation," and "resolution" don't describe factors interacting with one another.

The centers move goods from warehouses directly onto trucks so that trucks fill in minutes; the goal is to move as much material through the facility as quickly as possible. That rate is called throughput. Nothing in the text is about staffing, overhead costs, or liability.

The second sentence calls these things "quantifiable inputs," such as demand patterns and capacity constraints. Measurable inputs that shape a result are parameters. "Predictions" and "optimizations" are outputs rather than inputs, and "anomalies" are unusual events, which doesn't fit the examples.

The Phoenix example shows a character destroying a planet to illustrate "the corrupting influence of power," which makes the portrayal a warning. Warnings are admonitions. "Venerations" (honors) and "exonerations" (clearing of blame) are the opposite, and "obfuscations" means confusing things, which doesn't fit.

The underlined sentence describes what happens: expelled material arcs back to the Sun's surface. The rest of the text explains why: the gas, though fast, isn't fast enough to escape the Sun's gravity and magnetic field. D is tempting, but the later sentences explain the cause of the arc, not consequences that follow from it.

fix.passage: Research on minor solar eruptions in magnetically quiet regions revealed an interesting pattern. <u>Material expelled during these events follows a narrow arc trajectory back to the Sun’s surface.</u> High-resolution images show these eruptions produce thin streams of hot gas moving at speeds between 55 and 200 kilometers per second. Although these are impressive speeds, they are not sufficient to overcome the confining forces of the Sun’s gravity and magnetic field, so the material is pulled back down.

That is D. The text doesn't compare the formation of two specific holes (A, B), and it doesn't focus on one hole's formation (C).

In Text 2, the author feels his own consciousness flowing through the plants, including "the rustling palm leaves," showing close identification. A gets Text 1 backwards: the palms there are what home is contrasted with.

explanation: Frederick argues that clues inside the riddles (words like "here" and "now," the refrain asking for an answer, speakers acting as their solutions) point to an interactive, live performance, even though people today mostly read them as written texts. B captures both parts. A overstates the claim with "mainly performed at large public gatherings," and D invents newly found historical documents.

The Mexican s is pronounced with more tongue tension than the Castilian s, and Hidalgo argues it came from Nahuatl, replacing the Castilian sound. For that to work, the Nahuatl s must also have had more tension than the Castilian s. C reverses the direction of influence, and A and B make claims the text doesn't support.

fix.passage: In the Mexican dialect of Spanish, the consonant s is pronounced with greater tension in the tongue than it is in Castilian, the dominant dialect in Spain, resulting in a sharper sound. Margarita Hidalgo, a linguist at San Diego State University, argues that Mexican Spanish acquired this pronunciation from Nahuatl, the language of the Nahua people in Mexico: as the Spanish colonizers of Mexico incorporated Nahuatl words into their speech, and as more and more Nahuas spoke Spanish as a second language, the Nahuatl pronunciation of the s consonant replaced the Castilian pronunciation.

explanation: Don and his coauthor concluded that cover crops meaningfully increase soil carbon storage. If fields with cover crops for several years have much higher SOC stocks than fields without them, that directly supports the conclusion. A compares teff alone vs. in mixes, B describes reduced performance, and C is about variability rather than amount, so none of these supports the claim as well.

The text says comprehension draws on extra brain areas depending on what is being described: motor areas for physical actions, emotional areas for emotional accounts. So which combination of regions is used depends on the full context of the speech. B and C make specific claims the text doesn't support, and D adds that the combination may be "impossible to determine," which the text never suggests.

Molecular analysis doesn't depend on spotting subtle physical differences, while Discantenna metallica was identified by morphology alone, which does. So DNA analysis should be better at telling apart species that look very similar but are actually different. B is wrong because the text says DNA analysis avoids physiological detail rather than providing more of it, and C mixes up which species was identified by which method.

Text 1 describes the older idea that sauropods held their necks upright like giraffes. Text 2's simulations suggest sauropod vertebrae couldn't support a sustained vertical posture, and Kent argues they swept their necks horizontally. So the author of Text 2 would dispute the vertical-neck claim. The other choices aren't mentioned in Text 2.

In temperate forests, rarer species are more clustered with their own kind (the strongly negative correlation), so they face more competition from conspecifics and lose the rare-species advantage. Niche distinction would reduce the risk if those rare species can live on resources other species don't use much. C says exactly this. B contradicts the text by claiming temperate rare species benefit from RSA more than tropical ones.

"Despite its apparent pessimism" must be followed by the thing that seems pessimistic: the premortem activity. Only B makes "this activity" the subject right after the modifier. A, C, and D put the subject as "effective uncovering," "potential problems," or "teams," creating a dangling modifier.

The subject is the plural "achievements" (not "Bannister" or "barrier"), so the verb must be plural. The colon then explains his later medical career, so past tense fits: "weren't confined." "Isn't," "hasn't been," and "wasn't" are all singular.

Because one item contains internal commas, all items must be separated by semicolons, so a semicolon goes after "target." A comma (D) would be inconsistent, and a period (C) would leave a fragment.

A finite verb like "sought," "had sought," or "were seeking" would give the sentence two main verbs with no conjunction.

explanation: India has more English speakers than almost any country, yet only about 10% of Indians speak English. The first clause says the researchers did not study all North American ungulates; the second says they focused only on elk in Wyoming. Moving from what they didn't do to what they did is a contrast, so "however" fits. "For instance" and "in other words" don't fit a contrast, and "regardless" makes no sense here.

The system classifies instruments by how they make sound, and the saraswati veena makes sound through vibrating strings. It follows that the system classifies it as a chordophone. "Thus" signals that conclusion; "Furthermore" and "Similarly" just add information, and "Instead" signals a contrast.

B uses "Still" to concede the first point while noting the serial version matters for historical context. C just repeats the first sentence, and D introduces a claim about Eliot's intentions that the quotation doesn't support.
